summary: Specifies how authors of Independent Submission RFCs grant the community the rights to copy and use their text, and what rights the community grants to readers in return. It asks the IETF Trust to manage the rights. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you write something for everyone to read, you need to say what others may do with it. This document sets those copying rules for independent RFC authors.

subtitle: The copyright rules for Independent Submission RFCs: what authors grant, and what readers may do with the text.

tldr.problem: The Independent Submission stream needed formal procedures stating which rights authors give and which rights readers receive.
tldr.mechanism: Authors grant the same incoming rights as IETF-stream authors under RFC 5378, and the IETF Trust is asked to grant readers the right to make unlimited derivative works unless the document says otherwise.
tldr.outcome: Anyone may copy, extract, modify or use material with attribution, and authors can request a no-derivative-works restriction in special cases. The document updates RFC 4846.

today: RFC 5744 is an Informational document that updates RFC 4846. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
The Independent Submission stream continues the tradition of letting the RFC Editor publish documents relevant to the Internet community that are not products of, and do not conflict with, the IETF process. They may be comments on IETF documents or other relevant work.

RFC 5744 defines copyright procedures for these documents, in parallel with those for IETF documents in RFC 5377 and RFC 5378. It is meant to be fully consistent with Section 8 of RFC 4846 and updates it by clarifying the formal procedures the IETF Trust will use. The Independent Submission Editor (ISE) takes over responsibility for the stream, following RFC 5620.
sections.eli5: Some RFCs come from individuals outside the main committees. This note sets the copying rules for those, matching how the other RFCs work.

sections.title: Goals: A Liberal Copyright Policy
sections.content:
The stream aims to publish information that advances the state of the art and the interoperability of Internet solutions. The community decided a liberal copyright policy serves that best: any reader may use the content in any manner, with the only restriction being proper credit, or attribution. Lawyers call this permitting unlimited derivative works. The RFC notes it formalizes a 30-year-old policy followed by Jon Postel.

The policy covers all parts of a document, including code, so no separate license is needed to extract and adapt code from a document under the unlimited terms.

For a small subset, such as proprietary protocols or output from other standards bodies, authors may ask for a no derivative works restriction. Code cannot be extracted and adapted from those documents.
sections.eli5: The default is generous: use it however you like, just give credit. A few special documents can say 'look but do not remix'.

sections.title: How Authors Submit and Readers Use Material
sections.content:
Authors submit Internet-Drafts to the IETF Internet-Drafts repository like any IETF draft, and grant rights as described in RFC 5378. To ask for a no-derivative-works RFC, an author may use the form specified for RFC 5378.

The IETF Trust, in cooperation with the ISE, grants readers the right to make unlimited derivative works unless the document says otherwise. Drafts include boilerplate from the IETF Trust that indicates RFC 5378 compliance and states either that no derivative works may be based on the contribution or, as preferred, that unlimited derivative works are allowed.

Compliance is not a guarantee of publication. The final decision rests with the ISE, who may question a no-derivative-works request, and the matter is negotiated among the authors and the ISE.
sections.eli5: Authors tick a box saying how others may reuse their work, and the editor decides whether the paper gets printed at all.

sections.title: What Is Asked of the IETF Trust
sections.content:
The ISE asks the IETF Trust and its Trustees to publicly confirm that they can and will accept responsibility for the intellectual property rights of the stream and will work according to the procedures defined by the ISE.

The Trustees are asked to develop boilerplate so the Trust receives the rights specified in RFC 5378, and so documents can grant either no derivative-works rights or, preferably, unlimited derivative-works rights. How this is indicated in each document is left to the Trust.
sections.eli5: The editor asks the group that looks after the rights to write the standard wording and to take care of the paperwork.

sections.title: Patents, Trademarks and Security
sections.content:
Contributors follow the Internet-Draft process under the rules of BCP 9, then RFC 2026. This includes disclosing known or reasonably knowable patent and trademark issues, and, as requested by BCP 79 (then RFC 3979, updated by RFC 4879), disclosing license terms. The stream uses the IETF IPR disclosure mechanism.

The ISE prefers the most liberal terms possible, ideally without fees or licensing and non-discriminatory, but there are no specific requirements on licensing terms.

The Security Considerations say the integrity and quality of the stream are the ISE's responsibility, and this document does not change that.
sections.eli5: Authors must tell everyone about any patents or trademarks that might get in the way. The editor hopes for the friendliest terms, but does not force them.

left.title: Unlimited derivative works
left.desc: Preferred. Copy, extract, modify or use the text, including code, with attribution.

right.title: No derivative works
right.desc: Only on author request in special cases. Code may not be extracted and adapted.
